slides.title: Tables, types, keys and constraints
slides.text: Session 1 Tables, types, keys and constraints Name the type and the role of each column of a table Test a candidate key with a counting query Read the message a database gives when a constraint refuses a row 01

slides.title: A table holds rows of one kind, each with the same columns
slides.text: What a table is A table holds rows of one kind, each with the same columns return_id order_ref reason_code refund received_on T1 O-A11 R1 12.00 2026-05-02 T2 O-A12 R2 30.50 2026-05-02 T3 O-A15 R1 8.25 2026-05-03 T4 O-A15 R3 NULL 2026-05-04 T5 O-A20 R2 19.00 2026-05-06 The company's returns desk: the returns table. The slides use this department; the labs use the delivery tables. Unlike a sheet. No merged cells, no totals row, no colour that means something. Every fact sits in a column with a name.

slides.title: Every column has a type, and the type decides what fits
slides.text: Types Every column has a type, and the type decides what fits Type Holds Example VARCHAR text 'R1' INTEGER whole numbers 3 DECIMAL(8,2) exact amounts, two decimals 30.50 DATE, TIMESTAMP a day; a day and a time of day DATE '2026-05-02' BOOLEAN true or false true What goes wrong. An amount stored as text sorts as text: '9.00' comes after '30.50'. A date stored as text cannot be compared with a range.

slides.title: A key is a column, or a set of columns, that names exactly one row
slides.text: Keys A key is a column, or a set of columns, that names exactly one row A single-column key return_id in returns: no two returns share it. Declared as PRIMARY KEY, the engine refuses a second T3. A composite key (return_id, item_no) in return_items: a return has several items, so the return alone does not name an item; the pair does. Not a key. order_ref looks like an identifier, but one order can be returned twice: O-A15 appears in T3 and T4.

slides.title: Test a candidate key by counting rows and distinct values
slides.text: Proof, not belief Test a candidate key by counting rows and distinct values SELECT COUNT(*) AS n_rows, COUNT(DISTINCT order_ref) AS n_refs FROM returns; -- n_rows 5, n_refs 4 Equal numbers: no value repeats, the candidate holds Fewer distinct values: some value repeats, not a key For a pair, count the rows of SELECT DISTINCT a, b: 8 pairs for 8 rows of return_items Habit. Before you trust a key, count. It takes one query.

slides.title: A foreign key points at a row that must exist in another table
slides.text: Between tables A foreign key points at a row that must exist in another table return_items return_id T5 → returns row T5 must exist → reasons its reason_code R2 must exist Declared with REFERENCES returns (return_id), an item for a return that does not exist is refused. Without it, the item would sit in the table, joined to nothing, and every total would quietly miss it.

slides.title: Constraints refuse rows that make no sense, before anyone queries them
slides.text: Constraints Constraints refuse rows that make no sense, before anyone queries them NOT NULL The value must be there: every return has a received date. PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE No two rows share the value. REFERENCES The value exists in the other table. CHECK A rule on the value: qty > 0, refund >= 0. Type Only that kind of value: no text in a date. The message A refusal names the rule it broke. Read it.

slides.title: The grocery delivery company keeps its orders in six tables
slides.text: The case study The grocery delivery company keeps its orders in six tables stores Eight dispatch stores across five regions products The catalogue: names, categories, list prices customers Registered customers, with personal data orders Placed by a customer at a store, with a status order_lines Products, quantities, prices, discounts deliveries What happened when a courier went out Synthetic: January to June 2026, about a million order lines. People appear only as codes and roles.

slides.title: Which column is a key of return_items?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which column is a key of return_items? The returns desk's return_items has 8 rows. COUNT(DISTINCT return_id) is 5 and COUNT(DISTINCT product_ref) is 5. The distinct pairs (return_id, item_no) number 8. What names one row? return_id alone The pair return_id and item_no product_ref alone No column: the table has no key

slides.title: Six tables and their keys
slides.text: Lab 1.1 · 35 min Six tables and their keys List the six tables of the grocery delivery company, read their columns and types, test each candidate key by counting, and watch a key and a check refuse bad rows D1_1_tables_and_keys.ipynb List the six tables with their row counts 5 min Describe the columns and types of each table 7 min Test each candidate key: COUNT(*) against COUNT(DISTINCT key) 10 min Break a key and a check on the mini tables and read the refusals 8 min Write down what each table refuses and why 5 min ✱ Stretch: Find one column whose type is weaker than its meaning and say what that lets in

slides.title: Grain and cardinality
slides.text: Session 2 Grain and cardinality State the grain of a table in one sentence Confirm a grain with a counting query Measure a one-to-many relationship and name its maximum 02

slides.title: The grain is what one row stands for
slides.text: Grain The grain is what one row stands for returns One row per returned parcel return_items One row per item inside one return inspections One row per inspection of one return; a return can be inspected twice Say it in one sentence. "One row per ..." If you cannot finish the sentence, you cannot sum the table safely.

slides.title: A good grain sentence names the thing and the one it belongs to
slides.text: Writing it down A good grain sentence names the thing and the one it belongs to Vague Precise "Items" One row per item inside one return "Inspection data" One row per inspection of one return, on one day "Refunds by reason" One row per reason code, with the sum of refunds The precise sentence tells you the key: the thing, plus whatever tells two of them apart.

slides.title: Cardinality says how many rows of one table meet one row of another
slides.text: Cardinality Cardinality says how many rows of one table meet one row of another One to one Each return has exactly one decision letter. One to many Each return has one or more items. Many to many Products and returns: resolved through return_items. Write it as a range. "Items per return: 1..3" says more than "one to many": it gives the fewest and the most.

slides.title: Group the many side by the key of the one side, then read the smallest and largest group
slides.text: Measure it Group the many side by the key of the one side, then read the smallest and largest group SELECT MIN(n) AS fewest, MAX(n) AS most FROM (SELECT return_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM return_items GROUP BY return_id); -- fewest 1, most 3 What goes wrong. This query only sees returns that have items. A return with no item would not appear in the inner result, so "fewest" can never read 0 here.

slides.title: To see the zeros, count from the one side
slides.text: The zero case To see the zeros, count from the one side SELECT r.reason_code, COUNT(t.return_id) AS returns FROM reasons r LEFT JOIN returns t ON t.reason_code = r.reason_code GROUP BY r.reason_code; reason_code returns R1 2 R2 2 R3 1 R4 0 Reasons to returns: 0..2. Grouping returns alone would have said 1..2 and hidden R4.

slides.title: A join takes the grain of its finest table
slides.text: Looking ahead A join takes the grain of its finest table returns 5 rows, one per return → join inspections a return inspected twice appears twice → sum of refunds counts that refund twice Keep for Day 3. Before every join, write the grain of each side. If the result's grain is finer than the question's, aggregate first.

slides.title: What is the grain of the inspections table?
slides.text: Checkpoint What is the grain of the inspections table? The returns desk inspects some returns once, some twice, and some never. inspections holds return_id, inspected_on and result. Which sentence states its grain? One row per return One row per inspection result One row per return, inspected or not One row per inspection of one return

slides.title: The annotated schema
slides.text: Lab 1.2 · 35 min The annotated schema Write the key and the grain of each of the six tables, confirm them with counting queries, measure the cardinality of every relationship and check the annotated schema against the reference D1_2_annotated_schema.ipynb Write the grain of each table in one sentence 6 min Confirm each grain with a counting query 10 min Measure lines per order, attempts per order and orders per customer 10 min Fill in the annotated schema and run its check 9 min ✱ Stretch: List every join of the schema that can multiply rows, and the column that causes it

slides.title: Normal forms, wide tables and embedded engines
slides.text: Session 3 Normal forms, wide tables and embedded engines Explain the repetition that normal forms remove Build a wide analytical table from a join and name its risks Contrast an embedded engine with a client-server database 03

slides.title: Normalised tables store each fact once
slides.text: Normal forms, in brief Normalised tables store each fact once Form The rule, in plain words Returns desk example First One value per cell; no lists inside a cell Items in their own rows, not "X-101, X-205" in one cell Second Every column depends on the whole key The reason label is not in return_items: it depends on the return, not the item Third No column depends on another non-key column The label lives in reasons, reached through reason_code

slides.title: A fact written many times can disagree with itself
slides.text: Why it matters A fact written many times can disagree with itself Reason label copied onto every item Rename R2 from "wrong item" to "wrong product". Change 3 of the 5 rows that carry it and the table now holds both labels for the same code. Label stored once in reasons Change one row. Every query that joins to reasons sees the new label at once. The update anomaly. It needs no bug: only a partial fix, which is what busy people make.

slides.title: Analytical tables are wide on purpose
slides.text: The other side Analytical tables are wide on purpose Read far more than written : an analysis reads millions of rows and changes none Fewer joins for every question: the category and region already sit on the line Built from the normalised source on a schedule, never edited by hand Columnar engines store each column apart, so unused wide columns cost little to read The rule. A wide table is a copy. When it is wrong, fix the source and rebuild the copy.

slides.title: An embedded engine runs inside your program; a server runs apart and you connect to it
slides.text: Where the engine runs An embedded engine runs inside your program; a server runs apart and you connect to it Embedded A library in your Python process The database is a file Nothing to install or administer One writer at a time, on one machine Client-server A separate server process, often another machine Accounts, permissions, network Many users reading and writing at once Someone runs and backs it up The SQL you learn here runs on both, with small differences of dialect.

slides.title: Two embedded engines, built for different work
slides.text: The tool slot Two embedded engines, built for different work Analytical engine (DuckDB) Transactional engine (SQLite) Built for Scans and aggregates over many rows Many small reads and writes Stores Column by column, processed in batches Row by row In this course Every lab on the full data Lab 1.3 on the mini tables; lab 4.3 for indexes Examples of a capability, not endorsements. Either engine is free and runs on a laptop processor.

slides.title: The wide returns table shows two labels for R2. What do you do?
slides.text: Checkpoint The wide returns table shows two labels for R2. What do you do? The returns desk's wide table copies the reason label onto every item. A colleague renamed R2 in some rows only, so both labels now appear. What is the right fix? Correct the label once in reasons and rebuild the wide table Update the remaining rows of the wide table Add DISTINCT to every report on the wide table Delete the reasons table and keep the wide one

slides.title: One wide table, and what it repeats
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · 30 min One wide table, and what it repeats Join order lines to their order, store and product into one wide table, count what it repeats, make one copy disagree, and run the same count in a second embedded engine D1_3_wide_table.ipynb Build a wide table of order lines with store and product columns 8 min Count how often each store's region is repeated 6 min Change one region in the wide table and find the rows that now disagree 8 min Run the same count in the second embedded engine 8 min ✱ Stretch: Write two sentences on when the wide table is the right choice and who must rebuild it

slides.title: Filters, sorting and expressions
slides.text: Session 4 Filters, sorting and expressions Filter rows on text patterns and date ranges Sort with a tie-breaker and keep the top rows Compute a value per row with an expression that handles a NULL 04

slides.title: You write SELECT first, but the engine reads FROM first
slides.text: How a query is read You write SELECT first, but the engine reads FROM first 1 · FROM which table → 2 · WHERE which rows → 3 · SELECT which columns, computed how → 4 · ORDER BY, LIMIT in which order, how many Read in this order when you predict a result: start with the table, then cross out rows, then pick columns.

slides.title: WHERE keeps the rows for which the condition is true
slides.text: Filters WHERE keeps the rows for which the condition is true SELECT return_id, refund FROM returns WHERE reason_code = 'R1' AND refund >= 10; -- T1 12.00 Comparisons: =, <>, <, >= Combine with AND, OR, NOT; use brackets when you mix them A list: reason_code IN ('R1', 'R2') Text is in single quotes; column names are not

slides.title: = matches exactly; LIKE and ILIKE match a pattern
slides.text: Text = matches exactly; LIKE and ILIKE match a pattern Condition Keeps product_ref = 'X-101' exactly that code product_ref LIKE 'X-1%' codes starting with X-1; % is any run of characters label ILIKE '%item%' "item" anywhere, in any letter case LOWER(label) = 'late' "late", "Late", "LATE" What goes wrong. In DuckDB LIKE is case-sensitive: LIKE '%Item%' misses "wrong item". SQLite ignores case for plain letters: the same query behaves differently in another engine.

slides.title: Filter a period with a half-open range: from the first day, up to but not including the next
slides.text: Dates and times Filter a period with a half-open range: from the first day, up to but not including the next SELECT COUNT(*) FROM returns WHERE received_on >= DATE '2026-05-02' AND received_on < DATE '2026-05-04'; -- 3 returns: T1, T2, T3 What goes wrong. On a timestamp column, BETWEEN '2026-05-02' AND '2026-05-03' stops at the first instant of 3 May and drops the rest of that day.

slides.title: ORDER BY needs a tie-breaker before LIMIT can be trusted
slides.text: Sorting ORDER BY needs a tie-breaker before LIMIT can be trusted SELECT return_id, received_on FROM returns ORDER BY received_on DESC, return_id LIMIT 2; -- T5 2026-05-06 -- T4 2026-05-04 DESC from the highest; ascending is the default T1 and T2 share a date: without return_id their order is not defined LIMIT n keeps the first n rows after sorting

slides.title: An expression computes a new value for each row
slides.text: Expressions An expression computes a new value for each row SELECT return_id, COALESCE(refund, 0) AS refund_or_zero, date_trunc('month', received_on) AS month, UPPER(reason_code) AS code FROM returns; Arithmetic: qty * price COALESCE(x, 0): x, or 0 when x is NULL; T4 shows 0.00 date_trunc('month', d): the first day of d's month AS name names the new column What goes wrong. refund - 1 on T4 is NULL, not -1: anything combined with NULL is NULL.

slides.title: Write your prediction before you run the query
slides.text: The habit of the course Write your prediction before you run the query How many rows? One, a handful, about a sixth of the table Roughly what value? An order of magnitude, a sign, a range Which first row? After the sort you asked for Why. A result that surprises you is either a discovery or a bug. Without a prediction you cannot tell that you were surprised.

slides.title: Which filter counts every inspection made in May 2026?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which filter counts every inspection made in May 2026? The returns desk stores inspected_at as a TIMESTAMP. You need every inspection of May 2026, including those late on 31 May. inspected_at BETWEEN '2026-05-01' AND '2026-05-31' inspected_at LIKE '2026-05%' inspected_at >= '2026-05-01' AND inspected_at < '2026-06-01' inspected_at >= '2026-05-01' AND inspected_at <= '2026-06-01'

slides.text: Lab 1.4 · 35 min Questions 1 to 4, predicted first Write a prediction, then the query, for the first four of the twenty business questions: text filters, a date range, a sorted top ten and a line value; save them to your answer file D1_4_questions_1_to_4.ipynb Read the four questions and write a prediction for each 5 min Answer questions 1 and 2: a text filter and a date range 12 min Answer questions 3 and 4: a sorted top ten and a line value 12 min Compare each result with your prediction and save the part file 6 min ✱ Stretch: Rewrite question 2 with a half-open date range and explain why it is safer than BETWEEN

slides.title: Three things to keep from Day 1
slides.text: Wrap-up Three things to keep from Day 1 Count, then trust A key is proven by COUNT(*) against COUNT(DISTINCT). Say the grain "One row per ..." before every sum and every join. Predict first Rows, value or first row, written before you run.

slides.title: One table, then two
slides.text: Today One table, then two Session 1 · CASE expressions and set operations CASE turns rules into columns; UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT combine whole result sets Session 2 · NULL and three-valued logic NULL is unknown, not zero or empty: comparisons with it are neither true nor false Session 3 · Grouping and having GROUP BY changes the grain of the result; HAVING filters groups after they are formed Session 4 · Inner, outer, semi and anti joins Which rows survive a join, and how to ask for rows that have, or lack, a partner

slides.title: Which statement about the returns desk's tables is right?
slides.text: Review of Day 1 Which statement about the returns desk's tables is right? returns has 5 rows and 4 distinct order_ref values; inspections can hold two rows for one return. order_ref is a key of returns The grain of inspections is one row per return Joining returns to inspections can repeat a return A join to inspections keeps exactly 5 rows

slides.title: CASE expressions and set operations
slides.text: Session 1 CASE expressions and set operations Write a CASE expression that sorts rows into bands Count by condition with CASE inside an aggregate Combine two result sets with UNION, INTERSECT or EXCEPT 01

slides.title: CASE turns a rule into a column
slides.text: CASE CASE turns a rule into a column SELECT return_id, item_no, qty, CASE WHEN qty = 1 THEN 'single' WHEN qty <= 3 THEN 'few' ELSE 'many' END AS band FROM return_items; Branches are tried in order; the first true one wins ELSE catches the rest; without it, the rest is NULL Every branch returns the same type What goes wrong. Put qty <= 3 first and a quantity of 1 becomes "few".

slides.title: A CASE inside SUM counts the rows that meet a condition
slides.text: Counting by condition A CASE inside SUM counts the rows that meet a condition SELECT reason_code, SUM(CASE WHEN refund >= 15 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS large, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE refund < 15) AS small FROM returns GROUP BY reason_code; Two counts side by side, from one pass over the table FILTER (WHERE ...) says the same thing more briefly where the engine supports it A refund that is NULL is neither large nor small: count it on purpose if it matters

slides.title: UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT combine whole result sets
slides.text: Set operations UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT combine whole result sets UNION In either set, duplicates removed. UNION ALL keeps them. INTERSECT In both sets. EXCEPT In the first set and not in the second. SELECT product_ref FROM return_items WHERE return_id IN ('T1', 'T2') INTERSECT SELECT product_ref FROM return_items WHERE return_id = 'T5'; -- X-101, X-205: products returned in both groups

slides.title: Set operations compare whole rows, so choose the columns first
slides.text: The catch Set operations compare whole rows, so choose the columns first Too many columns SELECT * on both sides: two different returns never match, so EXCEPT takes nothing away. The column the question is about SELECT product_ref on both sides: the comparison is between products, as asked. Habit. Say "a set of what?" before writing either side.

slides.title: UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps every row
slides.text: UNION or UNION ALL UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps every row You want Use A list of distinct products returned in May or June UNION All return items of May and June, to sum quantities UNION ALL: duplicates are real items What goes wrong. UNION under a sum silently merges two identical items of different returns, and the total shrinks.

slides.title: Which query lists products returned in May but not in June?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which query lists products returned in May but not in June? The returns desk wants the distinct product codes returned in May 2026 that were not returned in June 2026. May's product codes EXCEPT June's product codes May's item rows EXCEPT June's item rows May's product codes UNION June's product codes May's product codes INTERSECT June's product codes

slides.title: NULL and three-valued logic
slides.text: Session 2 NULL and three-valued logic Predict the rows a comparison with NULL keeps Use IS NULL, COALESCE and IS DISTINCT FROM on purpose Explain why NOT IN with a NULL returns no rows 02

slides.title: NULL means unknown: not zero, not empty text, not false
slides.text: NULL NULL means unknown: not zero, not empty text, not false Unknown T4's refund has not been decided. Not applicable A line with no discount, in some designs. Not recorded A customer who gave no region. One marker, several meanings. The schema rarely says which. The business rule does: the finance rule of this course says an empty discount means none.

slides.title: A comparison with NULL is neither true nor false: it is unknown
slides.text: Three-valued logic A comparison with NULL is neither true nor false: it is unknown Condition on T4 (refund NULL) Result Kept by WHERE? refund = 12.00 unknown no refund <> 12.00 unknown no refund = NULL unknown no refund IS NULL true yes WHERE keeps a row only when its condition is true.

slides.title: AND, OR and NOT carry the unknown through
slides.text: Combining unknowns AND, OR and NOT carry the unknown through AND false AND unknown = false true AND unknown = unknown OR true OR unknown = true false OR unknown = unknown NOT NOT unknown = unknown What goes wrong. NOT (refund = 12.00) does not bring T4 back: the NOT of unknown is still unknown.

slides.title: Three tools make NULL behave the way the question needs
slides.text: Saying what you mean Three tools make NULL behave the way the question needs Tool Use it when x IS NULL, x IS NOT NULL you ask whether a value is missing COALESCE(x, 0) a missing value means a known default x IS DISTINCT FROM y you want "different", with NULL treated as a value SELECT COUNT(*) FROM returns WHERE refund IS DISTINCT FROM 12.00; -- 4: T4 included

slides.title: NOT IN with a NULL in the list keeps no row at all
slides.text: The classic trap NOT IN with a NULL in the list keeps no row at all Written code NOT IN ('R1', NULL) → Means code <> 'R1' AND code <> NULL → Becomes something AND unknown: never true Use NOT EXISTS when the list comes from a subquery that might contain a NULL.

slides.title: Aggregates skip NULLs, except COUNT(*)
slides.text: Aggregates Aggregates skip NULLs, except COUNT(*) 5 COUNT(*) 4 COUNT(refund) 69.75 SUM(refund) 17.44 AVG(refund) AVG divides 69.75 by the 4 known refunds. If an unknown refund should count as 0, the question wants AVG(COALESCE(refund, 0)) = 13.95. The returns desk, 5 returns, one refund NULL (_tools/slide_examples.py).

slides.title: How many inspections does this query count?
slides.text: Checkpoint How many inspections does this query count? An inspections table has 6 rows. result is 'pass' in 3, 'fail' in 1 and NULL in 2. What does SELECT COUNT(*) FROM inspections WHERE result <> 'pass' return? 3 6 0 1

slides.title: Predict, then run: twelve NULL comparisons
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · 35 min Predict, then run: twelve NULL comparisons With the assistant off, predict the row count of twelve short queries on the printed mini tables, run them, mark each prediction and repair the ones that did not say what was meant D2_2_null_predictions.ipynb Print the mini customers and order lines 3 min Predict the row count of each of the twelve queries on paper 12 min Run the twelve and mark each prediction 8 min Rewrite three queries so they say what was meant 9 min Write the NULL rule you will keep 3 min ✱ Stretch: Show NOT IN returning no rows when the list holds a NULL, and the NOT EXISTS that does not

slides.title: Grouping and having
slides.text: Session 3 Grouping and having Predict the number of rows a GROUP BY returns Choose between WHERE and HAVING for a condition Count distinct values inside a group 03

slides.title: GROUP BY changes the grain: one row per group
slides.text: GROUP BY GROUP BY changes the grain: one row per group SELECT reason_code, COUNT(*) AS returns, SUM(refund) AS refunds FROM returns GROUP BY reason_code; reason_code returns refunds R1 2 20.25 R2 2 49.50 R3 1 NULL Five rows in, three out: one row per reason that occurs. R4 has no return, so no group.

slides.title: After GROUP BY, SELECT may show only group columns and aggregates
slides.text: The rule After GROUP BY, SELECT may show only group columns and aggregates Refused, or meaningless SELECT reason_code, return_id, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY reason_code: which of R1's two returns would the row show? Fine SELECT reason_code, COUNT(*), MAX(received_on) ... GROUP BY reason_code Read it as "for each reason code, tell me ...". Anything else needs an aggregate.

slides.title: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after
slides.text: WHERE or HAVING WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after FROM returns → WHERE refund IS NOT NULL → GROUP BY reason_code → HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 → SELECT, ORDER BY Without the WHERE, the reasons with at least two returns are R1 and R2. A condition on a single row's value goes in WHERE; a condition on a count or a sum goes in HAVING.

slides.title: COUNT(DISTINCT x) counts different values inside each group
slides.text: Counting things, not rows COUNT(DISTINCT x) counts different values inside each group Expression Counts Returns desk, all items COUNT(*) rows 8 COUNT(DISTINCT return_id) different returns 5 COUNT(DISTINCT product_ref) different products 5 What goes wrong. "How many customers ordered in May" with COUNT(*) counts orders.

slides.title: Group by an expression to get one row per month, week or band
slides.text: Groups of time Group by an expression to get one row per month, week or band SELECT CAST(date_trunc('week', received_on) AS DATE) AS week, COUNT(*) AS returns FROM returns GROUP BY week ORDER BY week; The expression in SELECT and in GROUP BY must be the same; the alias saves retyping it In DuckDB date_trunc returns a timestamp, even on a DATE: cast it to DATE for a clean label

slides.title: How many rows does this grouped query return?
slides.text: Checkpoint How many rows does this grouped query return? A table of 40 deliveries covers 6 couriers; courier K9 made only 1 delivery. SELECT courier_id, COUNT(*) FROM deliveries GROUP BY courier_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. How many rows come back? 39 5 6 0

slides.title: Inner, outer, semi and anti joins
slides.text: Session 4 Inner, outer, semi and anti joins Predict the rows an inner and a left join return on small tables Find rows without a partner with an anti join Keep rows that have a partner without multiplying them, with a semi join 04

slides.title: An inner join keeps only the pairs of rows that match
slides.text: Inner join An inner join keeps only the pairs of rows that match SELECT t.return_id, i.result FROM returns t JOIN inspections i ON i.return_id = t.return_id; -- 4 rows T1 once, T2 twice, T5 once: 4 rows T3 and T4 were never inspected: gone The ON condition says which rows belong together Two silent effects. Rows without a partner disappear; rows with several partners repeat.

slides.title: A left join keeps every row of the left table, matched or not
slides.text: Outer joins A left join keeps every row of the left table, matched or not return_id result T1 pass T2 pass T2 fail T3 NULL T4 NULL T5 pass returns LEFT JOIN inspections: 6 rows. The unmatched returns come back with NULL in every column of the right side. A right join keeps the right side; a full join keeps both.

slides.title: An anti join keeps the rows that have no partner
slides.text: Anti join An anti join keeps the rows that have no partner SELECT t.return_id FROM returns t WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM inspections i WHERE i.return_id = t.return_id ); -- T3, T4 "Returns never inspected", "products never sold", "customers who never ordered" Also written as a left join with WHERE i.return_id IS NULL Avoid NOT IN (subquery): one NULL in it empties the result

slides.title: A semi join keeps each row that has a partner, once
slides.text: Semi join A semi join keeps each row that has a partner, once SELECT COUNT(*) FROM returns t WHERE EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM inspections i WHERE i.return_id = t.return_id ); -- 3 Not the same as an inner join The inner join counted 4 rows: T2 twice. "How many returns were inspected?" is 3. EXISTS never repeats a row.

slides.title: Choose the join from the question's words
slides.text: Choosing Choose the join from the question's words The question says Join "each ... with its ..." inner "every ..., including those without ..." left "... that never ...", "... without any ..." anti: NOT EXISTS "... that had at least one ..." semi: EXISTS

slides.title: How many rows does the left join return?
slides.text: Checkpoint How many rows does the left join return? couriers has 4 rows. shifts has 7 rows: courier A has 3 shifts, B has 2, C has 2, D has none. How many rows does couriers LEFT JOIN shifts return? 4 7 8 28

slides.title: How many rows does this query return?
slides.text: Review of Day 2 How many rows does this query return? A branches table has 5 rows; 2 branches have no region. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM branches WHERE region NOT IN ('North', NULL). 3 0 5 2

slides.title: Join fan-out and double counting
slides.text: Session 1 Join fan-out and double counting Detect fan-out by counting rows before and after a join Aggregate to the right grain before joining Explain a wrong total from the grain of each table it joined 01

slides.title: A join to a many side repeats every row of the one side
slides.text: Fan-out A join to a many side repeats every row of the one side return_id refund inspection T1 12.00 pass T2 30.50 pass T2 30.50 fail T5 19.00 pass T2 was inspected twice, so its refund now sits on two rows Every column of returns is repeated, not only the key Nothing warns you: the query runs, the numbers look plausible

slides.title: Every sum over a fanned-out join grows
slides.text: Double counting Every sum over a fanned-out join grows 92.00 SUM(refund) after the join 61.50 the refunds of the inspected returns 30.50 counted twice. And T3 and T4 are gone: the join also drops rows with no partner. A fanned-out sum can be too high and too low at once. The returns desk (_tools/slide_examples.py).

slides.title: Count rows before and after every join
slides.text: Detect it Count rows before and after every join SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM returns) AS before, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM returns t JOIN inspections i ON i.return_id = t.return_id) AS after; -- before 5, after 4: rows were dropped AND repeated After > before: some rows repeat After < before: some rows lost their partner Equal is not proof: drops and repeats can cancel out, as they nearly do here

slides.title: Bring each side to the grain of the question before joining
slides.text: The fix Bring each side to the grain of the question before joining WITH insp AS ( -- one row per return SELECT return_id, COUNT(*) AS inspections FROM inspections GROUP BY return_id ) SELECT SUM(t.refund), SUM(insp.inspections) FROM returns t JOIN insp ON insp.return_id = t.return_id; -- 61.50 and 4: one row per return on both sides Or filter instead of joining. WHERE return_id IN (SELECT ...) or EXISTS keeps each return once.

slides.title: SUM(DISTINCT ...) hides fan-out by accident, and breaks on equal values
slides.text: A tempting shortcut SUM(DISTINCT ...) hides fan-out by accident, and breaks on equal values Looks right here SUM(DISTINCT refund) on the joined rows gives 61.50: T2's repeat collapses. Wrong tomorrow Two different returns with a refund of 12.00 collapse into one. The total is short, and nothing says so. Rule. DISTINCT removes duplicate values, not duplicate rows of the grain you meant. Fix the grain instead.

slides.title: Before every join, write the grain of both sides and of the result
slides.text: The habit Before every join, write the grain of both sides and of the result Left Right Result Sum left? return reason return yes return inspection inspection no return return (aggregated) return yes Each grain is "one row per ..." the word in the cell. "Sum left?": is it safe to sum the left side's money after the join?

slides.title: Why is the total fee too high?
slides.text: Checkpoint Why is the total fee too high? A clinic sums appointment fees after joining appointments (one row per appointment) to reminders (one row per reminder sent). Some appointments got three reminders. The total is 40% above the ledger. Fees left NULL are counted as zero The join drops appointments with no reminder Fees are rounded to two decimals Each fee is repeated once per reminder

slides.title: Questions 16 and 17: count once
slides.text: Lab 3.1 · 35 min Questions 16 and 17: count once See a sum grow when order lines meet delivery attempts, then answer two questions that need lines and attempts together without double counting; save them to your answer file D3_1_questions_16_and_17.ipynb Count rows before and after joining delivery attempts 6 min Write a prediction for each of the two questions 4 min Question 16: line value of orders that needed a second attempt 10 min Question 17: orders and attempts per store in one result 10 min Save the part file 5 min ✱ Stretch: Find the share by which the naive sum of line values overstates the true one

slides.title: Subqueries and common table expressions
slides.text: Session 2 Subqueries and common table expressions Use a subquery in WHERE and in FROM Write a query as a chain of common table expressions Check each step of a chain before trusting the last 02

slides.title: A subquery is a query inside another, used as a value, a list or a table
slides.text: Subqueries A subquery is a query inside another, used as a value, a list or a table Where Returns Returns desk example In WHERE x > (...) one value refunds above the average refund In WHERE x IN (...) a list returns that were inspected In FROM (...) a table items per return, then their average

slides.title: A correlated subquery is evaluated for each row of the outer query
slides.text: Per row A correlated subquery is evaluated for each row of the outer query SELECT t.return_id, t.refund FROM returns t WHERE t.refund > (SELECT AVG(r.refund) FROM returns r WHERE r.reason_code = t.reason_code); -- the average of its own reason The inner query refers to t, the row being tested "Above the average of its own group" is the typical use The same answer can be written as a join to a grouped table: often clearer

slides.title: WITH names each step, so a long answer reads top to bottom
slides.text: Common table expressions WITH names each step, so a long answer reads top to bottom WITH items AS ( -- step 1: one row per return SELECT return_id, SUM(qty) AS units FROM return_items GROUP BY return_id ) SELECT AVG(units) FROM items; -- step 2: 3.0 units per return Read it as a recipe. Each name is a table you could look at on its own. Several steps are separated by commas: WITH a AS (...), b AS (...).

slides.title: Run each step before you trust the last one
slides.text: The method Run each step before you trust the last one 1 · First step alone select from it; look at 5 rows; count them → 2 · Its grain one row per what? is a key unique? → 3 · Add the next step and repeat → 4 · The final select compare with your prediction

slides.title: Some rules live outside the schema, and the query must carry them
slides.text: Business rules Some rules live outside the schema, and the query must carry them What the schema says Columns, types, keys, a status column with three values. What it does not say Which statuses count as revenue, what an empty discount means, which date books the money. The finance controller keeps that in data/revenue_rule.md. A query that ignores it runs without error and returns a number nobody in finance would sign.

slides.title: Turn each point of a rule into one named step
slides.text: From rule to query Turn each point of a rule into one named step Returns desk rule Step Only returns with a decided refund decided AS (... WHERE refund IS NOT NULL) Book on the inspection date, not the receipt date booked AS (... JOIN inspections ...) Count a return once, even if inspected twice take the first inspection per return A parallel rule of the returns desk; the finance rule of the labs is yours to turn into steps.

slides.title: Where is the error in this chain?
slides.text: Checkpoint Where is the error in this chain? A hotel's chain: stays (one row per stay) joined to charges (one row per charge), then SUM(nightly_rate * nights) per month. The result is far above the ledger. The final GROUP BY month The join of stays to charges before summing stay values Using WITH instead of a subquery Multiplying rate by nights

slides.title: Partitions, ranking, lag and lead
slides.text: Session 3 Partitions, ranking, lag and lead Write a window with a partition and an ordering Choose between ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK at ties Compare a row with the one before it using LAG 03

slides.title: A window computes over related rows and keeps every row
slides.text: Window functions A window computes over related rows and keeps every row GROUP BY Five returns in, three rows out: one per reason. The detail is gone. OVER (...) Five returns in, five rows out, each with a value computed from its group. SELECT return_id, reason_code, refund, SUM(refund) OVER (PARTITION BY reason_code) AS reason_total FROM returns;

slides.title: PARTITION BY says which rows belong together; ORDER BY says in what sequence
slides.text: The two clauses PARTITION BY says which rows belong together; ORDER BY says in what sequence Clause Question it answers Without it PARTITION BY region Whose rows are compared? all rows form one window ORDER BY day Which row comes before which? ranks and LAG have no meaning Say the partition in a comment. "-- partition: one ranking per region, so ..." The window checker of the labs asks for exactly this.

slides.title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK differ only at ties
slides.text: Ranking ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK differ only at ties product (units) ROW_ NUMBER RANK DENSE_ RANK X-101 (4) 1 1 1 X-412 (4) 2 1 1 X-118 (3) 3 3 2 X-205 (3) 4 3 2 X-330 (1) 5 5 3 Returned units per product at the returns desk, ordered by units from the most.

slides.title: Rank inside each partition, then keep the first places
slides.text: Top N per group Rank inside each partition, then keep the first places WITH ranked AS ( SELECT reason_code, return_id, refund, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY reason_code ORDER BY refund DESC) AS place FROM returns ) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE place = 1; -- the largest refund of each reason What goes wrong. WHERE RANK() OVER (...) = 1 is refused: windows are computed after WHERE. Rank in one step, filter in the next, or use QUALIFY.

slides.title: LAG reads the previous row of the window; LEAD reads the next
slides.text: Neighbouring rows LAG reads the previous row of the window; LEAD reads the next return_id received_on days_since T1 2026-05-02 NULL T2 2026-05-02 0 T3 2026-05-03 1 T4 2026-05-04 1 T5 2026-05-06 2 received_on - LAG(received_on) OVER ( ORDER BY received_on, return_id) AS days_since The first row has no previous row: NULL. With a partition, every partition's first row is NULL.

slides.title: Which ranking keeps every tied product in a "top three"?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which ranking keeps every tied product in a "top three"? Sales per product in each region: in the West, two products tie for third place. The manager wants both shown, and the next product, if any, to be fifth. ROW_NUMBER() and place <= 3 DENSE_RANK() and place <= 3 RANK() and place <= 3 ORDER BY sales DESC LIMIT 3

slides.title: Window drills 1: top items per region
slides.text: Lab 3.3 · 30 min Window drills 1: top items per region Rank products within each region, compare three ranking functions at ties, and measure the days between a customer's orders with LAG; each partition explained in a comment D3_3_window_drills_1.ipynb Drill 1: the top three products per region by quantity 10 min Drill 2: ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK on the same ties 6 min Drill 3: days since the customer's previous order, with LAG 8 min Write the partition comments and save the drills 6 min ✱ Stretch: Return the top three per region with QUALIFY and with a subquery, and confirm they agree

slides.title: Running and moving aggregates
slides.text: Session 4 Running and moving aggregates Compute a running total that restarts in each partition Compute a week-on-week change with LAG over weekly totals Choose a ROWS or a RANGE frame when days are missing 04

slides.title: SUM with an ORDER BY in the window adds up as it goes
slides.text: Running totals SUM with an ORDER BY in the window adds up as it goes return_id refund running T1 12.00 12.00 T2 30.50 42.50 T3 8.25 50.75 T4 NULL 50.75 T5 19.00 69.75 SUM(refund) OVER (ORDER BY return_id) T4's unknown refund adds nothing: the total stays Add PARTITION BY month and it restarts each month

slides.title: For week-on-week change, aggregate to weeks first, then LAG
slides.text: Comparing periods For week-on-week change, aggregate to weeks first, then LAG 1 · Daily rows one row per store and day → 2 · Weekly totals GROUP BY store, week → 3 · LAG over weeks PARTITION BY store ORDER BY week → 4 · Change this week minus the previous What goes wrong. A first or last week with fewer days looks like a fall or a jump. Say so beside the number, or leave partial weeks out.

slides.title: The frame decides which rows a moving average uses
slides.text: Frames The frame decides which rows a moving average uses Frame Means ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW this row and the six rows before it RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAYS PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW every row whose date is within the last seven days They agree when every day has exactly one row. They part when a day is missing.

slides.title: With a missing day, ROWS reaches too far back; RANGE does not
slides.text: Missing days With a missing day, ROWS reaches too far back; RANGE does not received_on day's refunds 2 rows 2 days 2026-05-02 42.50 42.50 42.50 2026-05-03 8.25 25.38 25.38 2026-05-04 0.00 4.13 4.13 2026-05-06 19.00 9.50 19.00 No return arrived on 5 May. "2 rows" averages 6 May with 4 May; "2 days" averages only 6 May, the one day in its window that has a row.

slides.title: Which seven-day average is right after a closed weekend?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which seven-day average is right after a closed weekend? A pharmacy's daily sales table has no rows for two closed days. For each day, the report wants the average daily sales of the days that had sales within the last seven calendar days, that day included. AVG OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAYS PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AVG OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AVG OVER (PARTITION BY day) AVG with GROUP BY week

slides.text: Lab 3.4 · 35 min Window drills 2: weeks and seven days From the daily order table, compute week-on-week change per store, a running total within each month and seven-day averages that stay right across closed days; run the window checker D3_4_window_drills_2.ipynb Drill 4: weekly orders per store and the change from the week before 10 min Drill 5: running net sales per store within each month 8 min Drill 6: seven-day average net sales, ROWS against RANGE 10 min Save the drills and run the window checker 7 min ✱ Stretch: Fill the closed days with zero rows from a calendar and compare the three seven-day averages

slides.text: Wrap-up Three things to keep from Day 3 Count once Bring each side to the question's grain before joining. Build in steps Name each step, run it alone, carry the business rule. Windows keep rows Partition, order, frame: say each in a comment.

slides.title: Building and checking
slides.text: Today Building and checking Session 1 · Loading into constrained tables, and transactions Stage the raw file, sort out what the constraints would refuse, load the rest in one transaction, account for every row Session 2 · Views that limit what is exposed A view gives each reader the columns and rows the purpose needs, and no more Session 3 · Query plans and indexes EXPLAIN shows how the engine will run a query; an index changes a lookup, rarely a scan of everything Session 4 · Testing queries against known answers A query is right when it matches answers you worked out by hand on data small enough to check

slides.title: Which ranking gives the tied products the same rank, and leaves no gap after them?
slides.text: Review of Day 3 Which ranking gives the tied products the same rank, and leaves no gap after them? A bakery ranks products by units sold. Two products tie for second place. The next product should be third. ROW_NUMBER() DENSE_RANK() RANK() NTILE(3)

slides.title: Loading into constrained tables, and transactions
slides.text: Session 1 Loading into constrained tables, and transactions Write table definitions with keys, foreign keys and checks Load a raw file through a staging table and record each rejected row with its reason Group inserts, updates and deletes in a transaction and roll back on a failed check 01

slides.title: A constraint is a rule the database checks on every row, every time
slides.text: Constraints A constraint is a rule the database checks on every row, every time Constraint Refuses Returns desk example PRIMARY KEY a repeated or empty key a second T2 NOT NULL an empty value a return with no date REFERENCES a value with no row on the one side reason R9, which does not exist CHECK a value outside a stated condition a refund below zero What goes wrong. A rule written only in a document is checked by nobody. Written as a constraint, it holds for every program that writes to the table.

slides.title: Stage the raw file as text, give each bad row a reason, then insert the rest
slides.text: Step by step Stage the raw file as text, give each bad row a reason, then insert the rest 1 · Stage every row as text, numbered in file order → 2 · Reject a rule gives each bad row one reason → 3 · Insert the rest, cast to the table's types → 4 · Log read = loaded + rejected Takeaway. Straight into a constrained table, the load stops at the first bad row. Staged, you see them all at once.

slides.title: CASE gives each row the first reason that applies, so the counts add up
slides.text: A reject rule CASE gives each row the first reason that applies, so the counts add up SELECT row_no, return_id, CASE WHEN return_id = '' THEN 'missing key' WHEN ROW_NUMBER() OVER ( PARTITION BY return_id ORDER BY row_no) > 1 THEN 'duplicate key' WHEN reason_code NOT IN (SELECT reason_code FROM reasons) THEN 'unknown reason' WHEN TRY_CAST(refund AS DECIMAL(8,2)) < 0 THEN 'negative refund' END AS reason FROM stg_returns row return_id reason 1 T6 2 T6 duplicate key 3 (empty) missing key 4 T7 unknown reason 5 T8 negative refund 6 T9 The returns desk (_tools/slide_examples.py, stage-reject).

slides.title: A transaction keeps all its changes or none of them
slides.text: Transactions A transaction keeps all its changes or none of them BEGIN TRANSACTION; INSERT INTO returns VALUES ('T10', 'O-A30', 'R1', 4.00, '2026-05-10'), ('T11', 'O-A31', 'R9', 2.00, '2026-05-10'), ('T12', 'O-A32', 'R2', 6.00, '2026-05-10'); -- refused: R9 is not a reason ROLLBACK; 5 → 5 rows of returns, before and after T10 and T12 were valid, and they are not kept either. Then COMMIT makes every change of a transaction permanent at once. What goes wrong. Without a transaction, a load that fails halfway leaves orders without their lines, and July's reports count orders with no revenue.

slides.title: Every row read is either loaded or rejected with a reason
slides.text: The load log Every row read is either loaded or rejected with a reason File Read Loaded Rejected returns 6 2 4 Rejected by reason: missing key 1 · duplicate key 1 · unknown reason 1 · negative refund 1 The log is the evidence that nothing was lost silently A rejection upstream changes counts downstream: the items of a rejected return are rejected too

slides.title: What does this load log tell you?
slides.text: Checkpoint What does this load log tell you? A clinic's appointments file: read 500, loaded 480, rejected 15 (12 unknown patient, 3 invalid date). The load is complete and every row is accounted for The transaction rolled back 15 rows Five rows are unaccounted for The file was loaded twice

slides.title: Load the extracts and log every rejected row
slides.text: Lab 4.1 · 35 min Load the extracts and log every rejected row Define three constrained tables, stage the defective July extracts, give each bad row a reason, and log every file as loaded plus rejected D4_1_load_with_log.ipynb Write the three table definitions with their keys and checks 10 min Load the three extracts into all-text staging tables 4 min Write the reject rules for orders and order lines, each with a reason 10 min Insert the valid rows inside a transaction and write the load log 8 min Check that read equals loaded plus rejected for every file 3 min ✱ Stretch: Correct one rejected order with an UPDATE inside a transaction, roll it back and confirm nothing changed

slides.title: Views that limit what is exposed
slides.text: Session 2 Views that limit what is exposed Mark the personal-data columns of a table Label tables with classification levels under a stated rule Build a view that exposes only what an analyst needs, and test it 02

slides.title: A column is personal data if it can identify a person, alone or with others
slides.text: Personal data A column is personal data if it can identify a person, alone or with others Direct identifier Points to one person by itself: a name, a phone number, an e-mail address. Indirect identifier Narrows the group when combined: a date, an area, a key that links all of one person's records. Neither Describes a choice or the record, and identifies no one on its own. The returns desk's callback list: return_id, caller_name, caller_phone, area, received_on, callback_ok. Which is which? The Personal Data Protection Law treats data that identifies a person directly or indirectly as personal data.

slides.title: Give each reader the columns the purpose needs, and no more
slides.text: Minimisation Give each reader the columns the purpose needs, and no more The law asks that personal data be limited to the minimum necessary for the purpose (PDPL, Article 11, paragraph 3) The Minimum Personal Data guideline adds: restrict access rights to what each role actually needs A purpose is a question: "how many returns per area each week" needs no name and no phone An exact date can often become a week or a month; an exact year, a decade What goes wrong. "Give them a copy without the names" makes a second table to secure, forget and leak. A view is not a copy.

slides.title: A level says how much harm disclosure would do, and so how the data is handled
slides.text: Classification A level says how much harm disclosure would do, and so how the data is handled Level Impact Unauthorised disclosure has Top Secret high an exceptionally serious and irreparable effect Secret medium a serious effect Restricted low a limited negative effect, including on an individual; examples include personally identifiable information and detailed statements of individual transactions Public none none of these effects The four levels of the national Data Classification Policy, written for public entities. Data not yet classified is treated as Restricted until it is. In the labs, the grocery delivery company has adopted the levels as its own rule.

slides.title: A view is a stored query: readers see its columns, never the table behind it
slides.text: Views A view is a stored query: readers see its columns, never the table behind it CREATE VIEW returns_for_analysts AS SELECT return_id, -- kept: joins to items; still personal data area, DATE_TRUNC('week', received_on) AS received_week FROM callback_list; -- no name, no phone, no exact date -- the test: none of these may appear DESCRIBE returns_for_analysts; Grant the view, not the table. The analysts' role reads the view; the table stays with the desk.

slides.title: Restricted rows never go into a generative AI tool; the schema can
slides.text: Responsible use Restricted rows never go into a generative AI tool; the schema can Can go in What the company has labelled Public: column names and types, the written business rules, an error message, a query with no values from the data. Stays out Rows of a Restricted table, a view's output, a sample "just to show the shape", a screenshot of a result. Rule. Only Public data goes into a generative AI tool. Which descriptions count as Public is the company's own labelling, written down before anyone relies on it.

slides.title: Which view gives the analysts what they need, and no more?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which view gives the analysts what they need, and no more? A gym's members table: member_id, full_name, phone, birth_date, branch, joined_on. The analysts count members per branch and per age band. member_id, branch, age band member_id, branch, birth_date member_id, branch, birth_date, joined_on a copy of the table without full_name

slides.title: Label the tables and build the analyst view
slides.text: Lab 4.2 · 35 min Label the tables and build the analyst view Mark the personal-data columns, label each table under the company's rule, and build a view the analysts can query without names, phones or e-mail D4_2_analyst_view.ipynb Open the supplied July database 3 min Mark each customer column: direct identifier, indirect identifier or neither 8 min Label each table with a classification level and a reason 6 min Write the analyst view with only the columns the purpose needs 10 min Run the analysts' three questions on the view and test that the identifiers are absent 8 min ✱ Stretch: Write a second view for the delivery team and list what it needs that the analysts do not

slides.title: Query plans and indexes
slides.text: Session 3 Query plans and indexes Read the operators of a query plan from the bottom up Find where a filter is applied in a plan Predict when an index changes a plan and when it does not 03

slides.title: A plan is a tree of operators: read it from the bottom up
slides.text: EXPLAIN A plan is a tree of operators: read it from the bottom up Seq Scan returns, filter on the date · reasons → Hash Join on reason_code → Hash Group By by label, sum of refund → Projection the columns returned EXPLAIN SELECT r.label, SUM(t.refund) FROM returns t JOIN reasons r ON r.reason_code = t.reason_code WHERE t.received_on >= DATE '2026-05-03' GROUP BY r.label;

slides.title: The engine applies a filter as early as it can, often inside the scan
slides.text: Where the filter is The engine applies a filter as early as it can, often inside the scan In the returns plan, the date condition appears in the scan of returns, under Filters: Rows that fail it never reach the join: less to match, less to group The numbers after ~ are the engine's estimates, made before running, not counts A filter on the result of a group (HAVING) cannot move down: it needs the groups first What goes wrong. Reading the estimates as row counts. To count, run the query; to see the shape, read the plan.

slides.title: An index lets a lookup go straight to its rows instead of reading them all
slides.text: Indexes An index lets a lookup go straight to its rows instead of reading them all EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM returns WHERE order_ref = 'O-A15'; -- SCAN returns CREATE INDEX ix_returns_order ON returns (order_ref); -- the same lookup: -- SEARCH returns USING INDEX -- ix_returns_order (order_ref=?) SCAN : every row is read and tested SEARCH : the index leads to the matching rows A total over the whole table stays a SCAN with or without the index SQLite, from Python's standard library (_tools/slide_examples.py, index-scan-search). No timings: the plan's shape is what is stable.

slides.title: An index helps a query that picks few rows by the indexed column
slides.text: When it helps An index helps a query that picks few rows by the indexed column Query on returns, index on order_ref Plan Why WHERE order_ref = 'O-A15' search an exact value of the indexed column SUM(refund) over all returns scan every row is needed anyway WHERE order_ref LIKE '%15' scan a pattern starting with % has no place to jump to WHERE reason_code = 'R1' scan not the indexed column Takeaway. Analytical queries read most of a table, so they rarely gain from an index. Lookups do.

slides.text: Checkpoint Which query can an index on patient_id turn into a search? A clinic's appointments table, 2 million rows, an index on patient_id. appointments per month this year appointments of doctor D12 patients whose number ends in 42 appointments of patient P-1093

slides.title: Testing queries against known answers
slides.text: Session 4 Testing queries against known answers Build a small fixture and work out the expected answer by hand Write a test that compares a query's result with the expected rows Classify a failing generated query: fan-out, wrong grain or a missing business rule 04

slides.title: A query is right when it matches an answer worked out by hand
slides.text: Testing A query is right when it matches an answer worked out by hand 1 · Fixture tables small enough to print → 2 · Expected the answer on paper, from the rule → 3 · Run the query on the fixture → 4 · Compare pass, or find out why Takeaway. The expected answer must not come from SQL: another query can share the mistake.

slides.title: Most wrong totals are one of three mistakes
slides.text: Why queries fail Most wrong totals are one of three mistakes Fan-out A join repeats rows. Returns joined to inspections: T2's refund counted twice. Wrong grain The right sum at the wrong level: an average per item when the question is per return. Missing rule Well formed, but a business rule is left out: the desk's rule says a return with no refund counts as 0.

slides.title: The average refund per return: the generated query against the rule
slides.text: A test that fails The average refund per return: the generated query against the rule 17.44 AVG(refund): skips T4, whose refund is empty 13.95 by hand, with T4 as 0: 69.75 over 5 returns Test: FAIL. Kind: missing rule. The fix is one COALESCE; finding it took the rule and a fixture. The returns desk (_tools/slide_examples.py, test-avg-refund).

slides.title: Every generated query ships with its test and a judgement
slides.text: The verification note Every generated query ships with its test and a judgement Query Expected Got Test · judgement avg_refund 13.95 17.44 FAIL · missing rule returns_r2 2 2 pass · ok Generated SQL is a draft until it passes a test against answers someone checked by hand The capstone asks for the same: a test per question and a log of any generated SQL and how it was checked

slides.title: A generated query passes its test. What does that show?
slides.text: Checkpoint A generated query passes its test. What does that show? A pharmacy fixture has six orders, none with two delivery attempts. The generated revenue query matches the hand-checked answer. The query is correct on the full data It follows the rule on the cases the fixture holds; repeat attempts are untested Nothing: generated queries cannot be trusted The fixture is too small to mean anything

slides.text: Lab 4.4 · 35 min Ten generated queries against hand-checked answers Hand-check the answers of ten questions on the mini tables, run ten supplied generated-style queries through tests against them, classify each failure against the revenue rule and write the verification note D4_4_ten_generated_queries.ipynb Read the revenue rule and the ten questions 5 min Work out the expected answers on the mini tables by hand 10 min Run the ten queries through the tests 8 min Classify each failure: fan-out, grain or a missing rule 7 min Write the verification note with each test result 5 min ✱ Stretch: Ask an approved assistant for the same ten questions, given only the schema, and run its queries through the same tests

slides.title: Three things to keep from Day 4
slides.text: Wrap-up Three things to keep from Day 4 Refuse and account Constraints refuse bad rows; the log accounts for every row read.
